reference.source: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Named for its cardinal triad of ear (oto-, conductive deafness), palate (cleft palate) and digital (hand and foot) anomalies, caused by gain-of-function FLNA variants
Hand and foot findings include broad, short thumbs and great toes and a characteristic gap between digits, giving a distinctive appearance
Craniofacial features include a prominent brow, hypertelorism, a flat midface and a small jaw
Conductive hearing loss arises from ossicular abnormalities and is an early and consistent feature
As an X-linked disorder, males are more severely affected while carrier females show milder, variable features; the more severe type 2 in males can be perinatally lethal
It sits within the FLNA otopalatodigital spectrum alongside frontometaphyseal dysplasia and Melnick-Needles syndrome, sharing overlapping skeletal and extraskeletal features
Management is supportive, addressing cleft palate surgically, providing hearing support and offering orthopaedic care, with genetic counselling for the family
reference.pathophysiology: Oto-palato-digital syndrome is caused by gain-of-function variants in the X-linked gene FLNA, encoding filamin A, an actin-cross-linking protein essential for cytoskeletal organisation and cell signalling during skeletal and craniofacial development. Disturbed filamin A function alters the modelling of the skull, palate, middle-ear ossicles and the tubular bones of the hands and feet, producing the characteristic ear, palate and digital anomalies. The severity gradient reflects X-linked inheritance: hemizygous males manifest fully and, in the more severe type 2, may have life-threatening malformations, whereas heterozygous females are variably protected by X-inactivation. The condition forms one end of the FLNA otopalatodigital spectrum, explaining its clinical overlap with related disorders.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of syndromic conductive hearing loss with digital anomalies
Pierre Robin sequence as part of a broader syndromic cleft
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey documenting the digital and craniofacial anomalies
Audiometry and middle-ear assessment for conductive hearing loss
Palate examination and imaging to characterise the cleft
Skull imaging where cranial-nerve or foraminal concerns arise
FLNA molecular genetic testing with X-linked segregation analysis
Evaluation for extraskeletal (airway, urogenital, cardiac) anomalies in severe or type 2 disease
redFlags: Airway or feeding compromise from cleft palate and craniofacial anomalies in infancy
Severe multisystem malformations in males suggesting the perinatally lethal type 2 phenotype
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with type and sex: milder disease is compatible with normal life expectancy and intellect, whereas the severe type 2 phenotype in affected males may be lethal in the perinatal period; hearing loss and skeletal issues cause ongoing morbidity in survivors.
pitfalls: Not recognising the condition as part of the FLNA otopalatodigital spectrum and its X-linked inheritance
Overlooking early conductive hearing loss and delaying support
Failing to anticipate the severe type 2 phenotype and its perinatal risks in males
Missing associated extraskeletal anomalies in more severely affected individuals
